title: Digital-system failure is being reframed as a cross-border cascade risk requiring analogue fallback, shared warning, and coordinated resilience
source_unit: International Telecommunication Union, United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction, and Sciences Po Paris School of International Affairs, When digital systems fail: An expert report on the hidden risks of our digital world
geography: Global digital infrastructure and the cross-border systems that depend on communications, energy, finance, transport, healthcare, emergency response, and government services

risk_frame.value: large-scale digital disruption is a plausible systemic-risk scenario rather than only an isolated technical incident

dependency_scope.value: electricity, finance, transport, healthcare, communications, and government services depend on deeply connected digital systems

governance_gap.value: critical disruptions can spill across sectors, institutions, and borders faster than existing governance frameworks are designed to manage

observations.method: Expert co-creation process convened by ITU, UNDRR, and Sciences Po, combining technical, policy, disaster-risk, and academic expertise to make hidden dependencies and knock-on effects visible.
observations.uncertainty: The report is a preparedness and risk-framing exercise; it does not predict that a particular failure will occur, estimate a universal probability, or provide a causal evaluation of resilience interventions.
observations.subgroup: People and organizations dependent on digital communications and essential services, with distinct exposure for countries and communities with limited infrastructure redundancy or fallback capacity.
observations.counterinterpretation: A systemic-risk frame can improve preparation, but it may also prioritize infrastructure continuity over privacy, access, affordability, or democratic control of essential digital systems.

observations.period: 2026; modeled cascade magnitude from natural-hazard disruptions

secondary_spillover_share.unit: share of digital disruptions from natural hazards attributed to secondary spillover effects

affected_population_multiplier.unit: ratio of people ultimately affected to those initially exposed in the cited risk frame

cascade_logic.value: local infrastructure damage can propagate through tightly coupled digital and essential-service systems

observations.method: The report synthesizes cited research and expert scenarios to illustrate how secondary failures can dominate the eventual reach of a disruption.
observations.uncertainty: The figures are cited estimates with source-specific definitions and contexts; they should not be treated as a universal multiplier for every digital incident or geography.
observations.subgroup: Users of essential services, infrastructure operators, governments, firms, hospitals, financial institutions, and communities exposed to cascading service loss.
observations.counterinterpretation: Cascade estimates can clarify hidden exposure, but headline multipliers may obscure variation in network architecture, redundancy, response speed, and local preparedness.

fallback_erosion.value: analogue skills and fallback options have disappeared, weakened, or are no longer tested across sectors

unequal_redundancy.value: small island developing states and least developed countries can face more acute vulnerability where infrastructure redundancy is limited

service_consequence.value: digital disruption can turn a physical hazard into a humanitarian crisis when healthcare, emergency alerts, payments, or communications fail

observations.method: The report compares cross-sector dependency and resilience conditions through documented hazards, expert knowledge, and illustrative scenarios.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not provide a complete country ranking, household-level impact distribution, or assessment of how affordability and digital exclusion affect recovery capacity.
observations.subgroup: Low-redundancy countries, remote and island communities, people reliant on digital payments or alerts, patients, older adults, disabled people, and households with limited offline alternatives.
observations.counterinterpretation: Investment in analogue fallback and redundancy may improve resilience but can be costly, unevenly maintained, or inaccessible if it is not designed around actual community needs.

denominator.unit: priorities identified through the expert co-creation process

priorities.value: build the knowledge base; update risk frameworks; strengthen standards and analogue fallback; coordinate on acute vectors and societal recovery; build trust and shared situational awareness; deepen global collaboration

operating_shift.value: preparedness requires mapping dependencies and chain reactions before disruption rather than focusing only on incident response

coordination_requirement.value: early warnings need trust, shared awareness, and cross-border collective action to become useful

observations.method: The recommendations synthesize the report’s scenario analysis and expert co-creation process into a preparedness agenda.
observations.uncertainty: The priorities are recommendations, not an implementation audit or evidence that each measure reduces disruption at a known rate.
observations.subgroup: Telecommunications and infrastructure operators, public agencies, disaster-risk authorities, international organizations, firms, researchers, and communities responsible for continuity of essential services.
observations.counterinterpretation: Coordination and shared standards can reduce fragmentation, but they can also create new dependencies or centralize decisions without guaranteeing local voice or remedy.

related_sources.claim: Related UNDRR disaster-risk context for systemic risk, resilience, and cascading impacts.
Related ITU publication on digital-sector emissions, energy, and sustainability commitments.

boundary: This record adds a digital-infrastructure and public-systems trend linking interdependence, cascade risk, service continuity, analogue fallback, unequal redundancy, early warning, trust, and international coordination. It is an expert report and scenario-based preparedness framework, not a forecast, incident census, respondent-level dataset, household impact estimate, causal evaluation, or proof that the proposed priorities produce equitable resilience.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official ITU publication page and downloadable PDF were reviewed for the cross-sector risk frame, cascade estimates, fallback and unequal-vulnerability claims, illustrative-scenario boundary, and six preparedness priorities.
